title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Corpses—The Novel's Poisoned Gift

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate reading of one of the great Victorian novels.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1865, and it may be his most savage and his most brilliant.
It begins with a corpse in the Thames and a fortune built on dust heaps — and those two images never quite let you go.
Today we open with the novel's central poisoned gift: a vast inheritance that seems to corrupt everything and everyone it touches.
And to help us think through what Dickens is doing, I'm joined by three extraordinary minds.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar whose eye for how Dickens builds his effects sentence by sentence is, frankly, formidable.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant to be poor — or suddenly rich — in Victorian England.
And Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great fiction is ultimately about individual character — moral imagination at full stretch.
Let's begin where the novel begins — with money, and what it does to people the moment it arrives.
What strikes me first, every time, is the sheer architectural intelligence of how Dickens introduces the Boffin fortune.
He doesn't give us Boffin spending the money, or enjoying it — he gives us the flood of letters that descends the moment wealth becomes public.
It's a brilliant structural choice — wealth is defined not from within but from the outside, by the appetites it attracts.
And then Dickens gives us this extraordinary catalogue — listen to the rhythm of it:

"Fifty-seven churches to be erected with half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings, seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred children to be brought up on postage stamps."
The absurd precision of those numbers is doing everything — it mimics the grandiosity of the charitable appeals while exposing their complete unreality.
The comedy and the critique are completely inseparable — which is exactly where Dickens is at his finest.
Eleanor is right that the satire is structurally embedded — and from a historical standpoint, it's also forensically accurate.
The mid-Victorian charitable landscape was genuinely chaotic — thousands of overlapping funds, many of them operating essentially as rackets.
And the use of aristocratic names to lend credibility — that was absolutely standard practice.
Which is why that ducal letter is so precise in its comedy:
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Every word in that phrase is doing satirical work — the fatness, the privacy, the ducal seal on what is, as we learn, a lithographed form letter sent by the hundred.
The pretence of personal attention — from a duke no less — dissolves the moment Dickens reveals the production method.
Class performing intimacy it does not feel — that's a very precise diagnosis of how Victorian philanthropy could operate as social theatre.
Both of my colleagues have identified something real — and yet I want to resist the temptation to treat this passage purely as social documentation.
What Dickens is doing, above all, is a study of human nature under the pressure of sudden proximity to wealth.
The individual beggars in the following passage are particularly illuminating in this regard.
Dickens tells us of those who send in their scraps and call them documents —
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is wickedly exact — and it is a moral observation, not merely a sociological one.
These correspondents have dressed their desperation in the costume of legitimacy — and Dickens sees the self-deception with perfect clarity.
The comedy does not diminish the tragedy — it sharpens it.
Edmund's point about self-deception is crucial — and the range of beggar types Dickens invents to illustrate it is almost dizzying.
The inspired beggars, the nobly independent beggars, the beggars of punctual business habits who announce a precise time of self-destruction —
each category is a distinct comic character sketch compressed into a sentence or two.
Dickens is showing us a kind of infinite human capacity for self-justification — that's what the variety is mapping.
And what underpins all of it — the charity rackets, the individual beggars, the ducal form letters — is the foundational absurdity of the Boffin fortune itself.
Wegg, of all people, puts his finger on it when he reads out that later will.
The first John Harmon's rationale for his bequests is laid out with devastating economy:

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
The will of a man who never loved anyone is itself a kind of final contempt — dispersed outward into the great anonymous body of the state.
And it is from that poisoned root that the whole elaborate comedy of solicitation grows.
A poisoned root — that's exactly the right image to carry with us as we go deeper into the novel.
Money that comes from dust, through death, via a will written in contempt — and then watch what it does to every human being who comes near it.
Coming up, we'll look at the characters at the centre of this storm — the Boffins, and what sudden wealth actually costs them.

segments.title: Bella's Hunger: Tracing a Woman's Reckoning with Desire

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today's segment carries a title about Bella Wilfer's hunger — her reckoning with desire, money, and what she actually wants from life.
But Dickens, being Dickens, sets Bella's transformation against a world of extraordinary suffering and extraordinary goodness — and we're going to explore all of it.
I'm joined today by three voices who I think will push this conversation in genuinely surprising directions.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley teaches creative writing and is fascinated by the architecture of Dickens's sentences — the way a single image can carry a whole chapter's moral weight.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will keep us honest about what the institutions in this novel actually looked like from the street.
And Sir Edmund Leigh — a retired Oxford don who reads great novels as stories about individual character tested by circumstance, and who will keep us from straying too far into abstraction.
Edmund, I want to start with you — because several of the passages before us today are about characters in extremis: Riderhood, Bradley Headstone, even Jenny Wren.
What does Dickens gain by surrounding Bella's moral awakening with figures who are suffering so profoundly?
It is a structural and moral strategy that Dickens deploys with, I think, rather more intelligence than he is sometimes credited for.
Bella's story is fundamentally a comedy — in the classical sense, a movement from error toward self-knowledge.
But Dickens will not allow us to find that comedy easy or cheap.
Consider Bradley Headstone, who sits in the novel as a kind of terrible anti-portrait of ungoverned desire.
The prose describing him near the novel's end is almost geological in its horror.

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
That is not merely atmosphere — that is the portrait of a soul consuming itself from within.
Bella's hunger for money and status is a lesser form of the same disorder — which is precisely why we need Bradley in the same novel.
That image of the charmed flame is extraordinary — Dickens gives Bradley a kind of Gothic enchantment, as if his own fixation has become a curse laid upon him.
But what strikes me technically is the accumulation — 'deepening,' 'haggard,' 'whiter and whiter,' 'degenerating' — each word a ratchet tightening.
There is no single catastrophic word; it is the relentlessness of the series that destroys him on the page.
Now contrast that with Jenny Wren — who is also in pain, but whose imagination transforms pain into something radiant.
Dickens gives her a vision of celestial children — and the prose becomes almost liturgical.
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
That refrain — repeated, chanted almost — is Dickens doing something completely different with suffering.
Bradley's pain turns him to ash; Jenny's pain calls down angels.
I find Jenny Wren's vision deeply moving, but I want to resist reading it purely as aesthetic consolation.
She is a disabled child, effectively running a household, with a father she describes as her bad child.
Dickens understood — with the precise knowledge of someone who had been poor himself — that the imagination is often the only resource left to those whom society has absolutely failed.
The celestial children offer Jenny what no institution in this novel manages to offer anyone: unconditional welcome.
Which brings me directly to Boffin's satirical demolition of charity patronage — because Dickens is quite specific about how false institutional benevolence is.
Boffin's tirade deserves to be savoured in full.

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
The joke works because the accumulation is itself the satire — title upon title, each one more hollow than the last.
Giving five shillings purchases you the word Patron — which tells you everything about what charity meant in that world, and perhaps in this one too.
James is right that the institutional satire is pointed — but I'd note that Boffin himself transcends the very world he is mocking.
When Harmon — speaking with real ferocity, I must say — explains what he owes the Boffins, the language becomes almost inadequate to the feeling.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
'There are no words to satisfy me' — that parenthesis is the most Dickensian thing in the passage.
The narrator — or rather the character — acknowledges that language has run out, and that acknowledgement is itself the measure of the debt.
Bella's transformation, when it comes, is powered by exactly this discovery: that true goodness cannot be denominated in any currency she previously understood.
And this is where Lizzie Hexam becomes such a crucial mirror for Bella — because Lizzie's speech about Eugene enacts exactly what Bella is only beginning to understand.
Lizzie speaks of her love in the third person, which is itself remarkable — as if the feeling is too large to be claimed directly.
She says — and this undoes me every time —

"'Only put me in that empty place, only try how little I mind myself, only prove what a world of things I will do and bear for you, and I hope that you might even come to be much better than you are, through me who am so much worse, and hardly worth the thinking of beside you.'"
The syntactic triple — 'only put me,' 'only try,' 'only prove' — is an incantation of self-erasure that is simultaneously an assertion of tremendous will.
Lizzie gives everything away and in doing so becomes the most powerful person in the scene.
That self-erasure has a class dimension that I think we cannot simply call selflessness without complicating it somewhat.
Lizzie is a working-class woman declaring herself 'hardly worth the thinking of' in relation to a barrister who has done precisely nothing useful with his advantages.
Dickens asks us to read this as love — and it is — but the novel is also quietly furious about the social architecture that makes this the only form her love can take.
Meanwhile, Riderhood's accusation of Gaffer Hexam — delivered with that grotesque theatrical solemnity — shows us what the law actually offers working people.
He says, with absolute confidence and no evidence worth the name —
"The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
The rhetorical force of repetition mimics the certainty of law while exposing it as sheer assertion.
In this world, a man can be destroyed by someone who simply repeats himself with enough conviction.
James identifies something real — but I'd observe that Riderhood's speech also tells us something about the moral squalor of the man making it.
Dickens is not naive about institutions, but he is ultimately more interested in souls than in systems.
Riderhood accuses; Bradley degenerates in the firelight; Wegg schemes in the dust heap.
Each is an image of what happens to a human being when one appetite — for revenge, or lust, or money — is permitted to colonise the whole self.
Bella's journey is the inverse: she begins with one appetite — she wants to be rich — and gradually discovers that she wants, instead, to be good.
That distinction — souls versus systems — feels like the right place to pause, because it names the tension running through every passage we've looked at today.
Bradley consumed by fire, Jenny sustained by angels, Lizzie pouring herself out in love, Harmon searching for words that do not exist, Boffin mocking the whole edifice of charitable vanity.
Dickens assembles all of this around a young woman reckoning with what she actually desires.
In our next segment, we'll follow that reckoning closer — into the specific scenes where Bella begins, haltingly, to change.

segments.title: Dust, Wealth, and Corruption: What the Heaps Reveal

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — and examine what's inside.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with surfaces — with what things appear to be, and what they conceal.
Dust heaps that are actually treasure. Gentlemen who are actually furniture. Marriages that are actually licences to fight.
Today we're diving into questions of wealth, corruption, and social theatre — the machinery that sorts people into dining tables and dust.
With me are three people I trust implicitly to make sense of this extraordinary book.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose eye for craft is quite simply without equal in this room.
Professor James Blackstone brings legal and social history — the institutional bones beneath Dickens's satirical flesh.
And Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, reminds us that before all the sociology, this is a novel about human character — tested, broken, occasionally redeemed.
Let's begin with the novel's most brazen satirical gambit — the moment Dickens introduces a man by comparing him to a dining table.
The Twemlow passage is, for my money, the most economical piece of class satire in the entire novel.
Dickens doesn't call Twemlow a social climber, or a parasite, or a fool — he simply calls him a piece of furniture.
And then he sustains the metaphor with a kind of remorseless precision that is almost cruel.
The passage reads — and I want to give it its full weight — as follows.
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
The dining-table in its normal state — meaning without extra leaves, without guests added.
Twemlow, as the cousin of a lord, is the baseline social credential — the thing around which everything else is arranged.
And what's historically precise about this is that the Veneerings — new money, no lineage — genuinely needed men like Twemlow to legitimise their gatherings.
He's not a person to them. He's a function.
What I find almost giddily brilliant about it is the way Dickens extends the metaphor beyond any reasonable limit — and that excess is the point.
He gives us the leaves inserted, the table pulled to twenty leaves, Twemlow at one end near the sideboard or curtains — it becomes almost architectural.
And then comes the devastating final move: the more Twemlow is pulled out — expanded, used — the further he finds himself from the centre.
Social use doesn't bring you closer to power. It pushes you to the margins.
And Dickens buries this insight inside an extended joke about furniture, which is exactly where it belongs.
I don't dispute any of that — the satire is ferociously effective.
But I think we risk missing something if we read Twemlow only as a symbol of social mechanics.
Dickens introduces him as a piece of furniture, yes — but he also tells us he is kept over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street.
There is a man inside the metaphor — a man with a lodging, with modest circumstances, with the particular indignity of being stored away when not in use.
What Dickens is charting isn't merely class machinery but the experience of a certain kind of English gentleman — genteel, impecunious, harmlessly complicit in his own diminishment.
By the novel's end, Twemlow will be one of the few characters to say something genuinely decent.
Dickens is preparing us, even here, to understand that the furniture might have a conscience.
Edmund's point is well taken — Twemlow is being preserved, not destroyed.
But the contrast I keep returning to is between this world of social theatre and the far rawer world Dickens shows us through Pleasant Riderhood.
If the Veneering dinner table is a performance of social legitimacy, Pleasant's world shows us what happens when the performance was never available to you in the first place.
Dickens gives us her view of the world's ceremonies with a passage that is worth quoting at length.
"Show Pleasant Riderhood a Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular licence to quarrel and fight."
A wedding, a christening, a funeral — she reads each as a sham, because experience has made any other reading impossible.
Her father's duty to her, Dickens tells us, was always incorporated in the form of a fist or a leathern strap.
The social institutions that are merely theatre for the Veneerings are instruments of violence for people like Pleasant.
And yet — and this is what I find so extraordinary about that passage — Dickens doesn't end there.
He says: there was even a touch of romance in her.
After everything — the violence, the cynicism, the predatory relationship with sailors — a touch of romance.
He imagines her on a summer evening looking from the reeking street to the sunset, dreaming of far-off islands.
The craft move there is devastating in its gentleness: he's refusing to seal her inside her own damage.
She has been made by her circumstances — but she has not been entirely consumed by them.
That is precisely my point about Dickens, expressed rather better than I expressed it.
He is not a sociologist constructing a case study. He is a novelist attending to the inner life.
Pleasant Riderhood's dreams of bread-fruit islands are not offered as satire. They are offered as something close to dignity.
And that act of imaginative generosity is, I think, what separates Dickens from the merely polemical writers of his era.
From the drawing rooms of the Veneerings to the waterside of Limehouse — the novel keeps pulling us down through the social strata.
But there's one scene in the novel where wealth and cruelty collide in the most intimate possible way — the story of young John Harmon's departure.
James, you've been sitting with that passage — what does it tell us about money and childhood in this world?
This is one of the passages in the novel that I find genuinely difficult to discuss without a certain tightening in the chest.
Boffin is recounting the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon — a child of seven, being sent abroad alone.
The father — old Harmon — wouldn't hear of allowing a sixpence coach-money.
A man sitting on a fortune built from dust, and he begrudges his seven-year-old son sixpence for a cab to the steamboat.
Let me read what Boffin actually says, because no paraphrase does it justice.

"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat, as the old man wouldn't hear of allowing a sixpence coach-money."
Little scanty — twice in two sentences.
Boffin is not a literary man. That repetition is grief, not rhetoric.
And then Mrs Boffin — young, warm, described as a picture of a full-blown rose — kneels at the fire and rubs the child's cheeks to warm him, and weeps.
She cries: "I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
The Harmon money — the inheritance that drives the entire plot — originates here, in this moment of a child weeping and an old man counting sixpences.
What Dickens does with the look is remarkable.
Boffin says the boy looked up at them as if it was in pain — in agony.
And then he tells us that Mrs Boffin, for years afterward, could never shake that look — that according to her thoughts, he never changed it.
That's a devastating structural choice — the child's adult story is shadowed by a single childhood look that won't release its grip.
And notice how Boffin phrases the way it ended — it gently wore out, as many things do.
That's Boffin's voice — stoic, simple, heartbreaking — and it's Dickens trusting the character to carry the weight without authorial underlining.
Mrs Boffin's desire to shelter the child is one of the novel's great moral gestures.
She and Boffin remain childless — and we understand now that their childlessness has a specific emotional content, a specific face attached to it.
Boffin tells us that they decided against having a child of their own, because other eyes might see that lonely look in our child.
This is not a social programme. This is a moral imagination working at full power — the capacity to extend human sympathy beyond the self.
And it is, I would argue, why the Boffins remain among the most genuinely good people Dickens ever created.
From that tenderness, the novel turns — as it always does — toward something much darker.
James, you've been looking at the Riderhood and Bradley Headstone confrontation — perhaps the novel's most sustained piece of gothic menace.
What strikes me about the confrontation between Riderhood and Bradley Headstone is how purely transactional it is.
There's no ideological conflict here, no class warfare in the conventional sense — just one man who has evidence over another man, and intends to extract everything he can from it.
Riderhood lays it out with a kind of terrible, itemised precision.
"I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows.
I've got them, and I've got you."
That final repetition — I'll be paid for it, I'll be paid for it, I'll be paid for it — is pure extortion without any pretence of justice.
What makes it historically resonant is that Bradley Headstone — the schoolmaster, the self-made respectable man — is destroyed not by the law but by someone even lower in the social order.
His respectability was always a performance, and Riderhood watched the dress rehearsal.
The language Dickens gives Riderhood is extraordinary — spattered all over with what bust from the blows.
That circumlocution — what bust from the blows, rather than blood — does something a direct word never could.
It makes you supply the word yourself. The horror is more complete because you complete it.
And then tore this way and that way — the repetition of that phrasing has the same quality: you see the garment, you see the struggle.
Riderhood's speech is crude, but it's not clumsy — it's doing precise psychological work on Bradley.
I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master, where you sat down Bargeman.
That line haunts me.
Because what Riderhood is describing is not merely the removal of a disguise — it is the collapse of an entire self.
Bradley Headstone spent his life constructing respectability from nothing — from a poor enough beginning, as Dickens tells us elsewhere.
And the bargeman's clothes — the disguise chosen to commit the crime — are also, in some terrible sense, his original self.
The costume he wore to murder Wrayburn is the costume he wore before he became Bradley Headstone, Master.
What a way to put it — the disguise and the origin as the same thing.
In a novel about identities built from dust, that may be its darkest irony.
We'll return after the break to ask what, if anything, the novel offers as redemption — and whether Dickens earns the happiness he gives to some of his characters and withholds from others.

segments.title: The Man Who Isn't: John Harmon's Double Life

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great last completed novel apart, chapter by chapter, layer by layer.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's most daring structural conceits: the hero who is believed dead, wandering his own inheritance under a borrowed name.
John Harmon — presumed drowned, listed in the newspapers as a corpse — is in fact alive, installed in the Boffin household as the secretary John Rokesmith.
To help us unpack what Dickens is doing with this extraordinary device, I'm delighted to introduce our three guests.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a fine movement — for the mechanisms beneath the surface.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will keep us honest about what the world of this novel actually felt like from the inside.
And Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who insists, with considerable force, that great novels are ultimately about individual souls, not social systems.
Welcome, all three of you.
Now — Dickens himself breaks cover in a remarkable authorial aside late in the novel to address exactly what he was doing with the Harmon mystery.
Eleanor, shall we start there — with the author's own account of his design?
Yes — and it is a fascinatingly unusual moment, because Dickens steps out from behind the curtain of the fiction to speak directly to us about craft.
He says — and this is in the text itself —

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
What I love about that is the almost paradoxical precision of it: he was hiding in plain sight.
The mystery isn't a puzzle to be solved — it's a dramatic irony to be felt.
And then Dickens does something rather bold — he asks the reader to trust the artist's judgment, to grant him patience with the design.
That's a remarkable request in a serialised novel, where readers are meeting fragments week by week with no certainty about where the whole is going.
The authorial intrusion is interesting, but I think we should be careful not to over-weight it.
Dickens is defending himself against impatient critics — that is all.
What matters to me is not the mechanics of narrative disclosure, but why John Harmon's concealment is morally necessary to him.
He returns to a world in which his father made him a commodity — a piece of property to be disposed of along with the dust heaps.
Before he can inherit, he needs to know whether he can trust the world that inheritance places him in.
The disguise is an act of self-preservation, yes — but it is also, in the deepest sense, an act of moral scrutiny.
Edmund's point about trust is well taken, but I'd ground it more specifically in what John Harmon is actually returning to.
His father was a man who accumulated vast wealth through the dust trade — refuse collection, essentially — and ruled his household with something approaching tyranny.
The passage where Boffin describes what the old man was actually like is extraordinary in that regard.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet... and send it spinning across the yard... and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repeated 'Dropped her' is devastating in its plainness.
This is a household where physical violence was the currency of authority — and it was a household John Harmon was legally bound to.
The will, remember, compelled him to marry a woman he had never met as the condition of his inheritance.
James, that repetition — 'Dropped her. Dropped her' — it's Dickens doing something quite precise with Boffin's voice.
Boffin's speech is folksy, compressed, grammatically unusual — and yet that compression carries an enormous weight of witnessed suffering.
The sentence drops to two words because the event itself dropped Mrs Boffin.
The syntax enacts the action — and that's Dickens at his most instinctive and powerful.
I would add that the Boffins are not merely witnesses to old Harmon's cruelty — they are its antithesis, and that contrast is structurally essential.
Consider what the novel tells us about why old Harmon named them in his will at all.
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
The miser recognises virtue precisely because he cannot corrupt it.
There is something almost classical in that — the tyrant bearing involuntary witness to the goodness he has failed to destroy.
It is not a social argument — it is a moral portrait, and a rather magnificent one.
Edmund reads it as moral portrait — and I don't dispute that — but the novel is also being precise about how incorruptible servants actually fare under such a system.
The Boffins are called 'every name he could lay his tongue to' — the recompense for honesty, under old Harmon, is abuse.
The will is not a reward system — it is an accident of a tyrant's self-knowledge, arriving too late to do John Harmon any good.
Which is, of course, Boffin's own bitter observation at the start — the poor boy gets no good of it.
And into that absence — that void where John Harmon should have been — Mrs Boffin proposes something deeply touching.
She wants to find an orphan, name him John, and give the money a living shape.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
The irony is extraordinary — she wants to resurrect John Harmon symbolically, not knowing that the real John Harmon is about to reappear in their midst.
Memory, identity, substitution — the novel turns all of these simultaneously in this one small domestic scene.
Yes — and what makes it affecting rather than sentimental is the precise ordinariness of how Mrs Boffin frames it.
'Say it's only a whim' — she is pre-emptively apologising for her own goodness.
There is no rhetoric, no self-congratulation — just a quiet human impulse trying to make right what cannot be made right.
What's remarkable is that the novel keeps these threads in motion simultaneously — the identity question, the moral weight of the Boffins, the ghostly presence of the 'dead' heir.
Before we move on, I want to bring in one more image — because Dickens places two other characters, Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren, in a rooftop garden tended by the Jewish moneylender Riah.
James — what do you make of that scene, and what does it say about the novel's understanding of refuge?
It is one of the most quietly surprising images in the whole novel.
Two women from the margins of respectable society — a waterman's daughter and a crippled doll's dressmaker — are reading, studying, growing things on a rooftop above the city.
And the passage is careful about this:
"Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet... they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces."
What strikes me is that 'attentive faces' — these are not passive recipients of charity; they are actively learning, reaching toward something.
The rooftop garden is a kind of pocket of the world as it might be — above the smoke and the grime and the machinery of class.
The prose around that scene is doing something extraordinary — the chimneys are described as 'bridling, and fanning themselves, and looking on in a state of airy surprise.'
The industrial world is personified — and it is surprised by what it sees.
Dickens gives us a pastoral idyll in the middle of London's grimiest district, and then has the landscape itself register astonishment.
It connects, I think, to the Harmon story — because John Harmon too is a kind of impossible presence, a figure who shouldn't be there but is.
I am rather struck by the fact that both scenes — Mrs Boffin's wish for a renamed orphan, and the rooftop garden — are acts of imaginative remaking.
Identity in this novel is not fixed by birth or name — it is something that can be given, borrowed, or grown toward.
That is, I would argue, the deepest thing Dickens is saying through John Harmon's disguise — not that identity is unstable, but that it must be earned.
Earned — that's a word I suspect we'll keep returning to as we move deeper into this novel.
Identity earned, virtue tested, money as a force that reveals rather than creates character — all of it in motion from these earliest chapters.
Thank you, Eleanor, James, Edmund — and we'll be back shortly to look at how the novel's great river continues to do its work.

segments.title: Kindness and Suspicion: Boffin's Moral Pivot

utterances.text: We turn now to one of the novel's most intricate moral territories — the question of disguise, and what it costs.
John Harmon is alive, hidden, watching — and the deception he set in motion has taken on a life entirely its own.
Eleanor, James, Edmund — I want to begin with the architecture of Harmon's original scheme, because it's stranger and more morally ambiguous than it first appears.
What strikes me immediately is how Dickens constructs Harmon's confession as a kind of recursive audit — he keeps checking his own memory.
The phrase 'I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right' — that compulsive self-verification tells us everything about his psychological state.
But what's structurally brilliant is that Dickens gives us the scheme in Harmon's own voice, with all its naive optimism still intact.
He wanted to put himself in Bella Wilfer's way before she could know him for himself — to see her clear, without the distorting lens of money.
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
It's almost touchingly amateur — two men in costume, lurking in Limehouse, hoping that chance will be kind.
And yet Dickens never lets us laugh too long, because the stakes underneath are entirely serious.
The scheme is amateur, yes — but Eleanor, I'd push back slightly on the innocence we're granting it.
Harmon is, in legal terms, a man who has allowed himself to be declared dead while remaining very much alive and in possession of full faculties.
The consequences for the Boffins — who have acceded to the fortune in good faith — are substantial.
Dickens is quite clear about what drives the decision to stay dead.
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving Bella.' That's not sentiment — that's a test, conducted on a woman who has no knowledge she is being examined.
The social historian in me notices that such surveillance of women's character was entirely normalised in Victorian courtship — which makes it no less troubling.
James is right to flag the discomfort — but I think we must weigh it against the particular anguish Harmon is navigating.
Dickens gives us, in the thirty-first chapter, one of the most penetrating diagnoses of moral paralysis in the whole of Victorian fiction.
The deception, we're told, began from a place of genuine good faith.
'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood... he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.'
That accumulation — 'a few hours or days' — is Dickens showing us precisely how moral compromises expand to fill the space available.
The question is not whether Harmon acted wisely, but whether he acted from a recognisably good impulse corrupted by circumstance.
I believe Dickens intends us to say: yes, he did.
Edmund, I find that deeply persuasive — and yet it leaves me with a structural puzzle.
Because Dickens stages the impossible bind so precisely — by coming to life and accepting the inheritance, Harmon must buy Bella; by coming to life and rejecting it, he must punish her.
There is no exit from that logic that doesn't damage someone.
And the dread of the father's money is articulated with real force.
'The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil.'
That sentence is doing extraordinary work — it connects the personal, the familial, and the almost mythic in one sweep.
The Harmon fortune isn't just an inheritance — it's a curse that needs to be broken, and Harmon knows it.
That word 'perpetuating' is doing considerable work historically as well.
Dickens understood, better than most of his contemporaries, that inherited wealth was not merely a financial instrument but a moral inheritance — for good or ruin.
And the novel plants that same dread at a different register entirely when Lizzie describes the child surrounded by alcoholics.
The inheritance there is not money but degradation, handed down as reliably as any fortune.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthetical — 'if she ever had one' — is a blade, quietly inserted.
The cradle — that most basic symbol of care and beginning — may never have existed for this child.
Dickens knows exactly where to press.
James has reminded me that Dickens never lets the weight of the grand theme crush the comic.
In the very same chapters, we have Sloppy, in his new black suit — an occasion for Dickens at his most purely delightful.
The tailor's art has been deployed, we're told, with 'the utmost cunning' to conceal Sloppy's structural infelicities — and has failed comprehensively.
'he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.'
The Argus myth — the hundred-eyed giant — deployed in service of a badly fitting suit.
Only Dickens would reach for Greek mythology to describe a young man's buttons.
And yet the comedy is never at Sloppy's expense in any cruel sense — it's at the expense of tailoring pretension and social ceremony.
Sloppy himself remains perfectly dignified throughout.
Edmund is absolutely right about that — the comedy illuminates class without diminishing the person.
The 'imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted' at Sloppy's hatband — that's Dickens mocking the language of aesthetic judgment, not Sloppy.
And it rhymes, structurally, with Harmon's predicament — both men are trying to present themselves in a form society will accept.
Sloppy's buttons refuse to be concealed; Harmon's identity refuses to stay buried.
Dickens is always doing at least two things at once.
That structural parallel is a beautiful note to rest on — the body that won't conform, and the self that won't stay dead.
We've moved through disguise, inherited fate, and a suit that defies all human tailoring — and what connects them, I think, is the question of what can be concealed and for how long.
When we return, we'll turn to how the novel's women — Bella above all — respond to precisely that question.

segments.title: Dickens's Architecture: How the Novel Holds Its Weight

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been talking about the world Dickens builds in this novel — its rivers, its dust heaps, its social machinery.
Now we want to step back and ask a bigger question: how does the novel actually hold together?
What are the structural and narrative choices that give Our Mutual Friend its remarkable coherence and weight?
Eleanor Hartley is perfectly placed to guide us here — as a novelist herself, she reads Dickens with a craftsperson's eye.
Eleanor, let's begin with those very first pages — with Gaffer Hexam on the river.
Thank you — because those opening pages are, to my mind, one of the most audacious beginnings in all of English fiction.
Dickens doesn't open with an explanation or a character introduction in any conventional sense.
He opens with sensation — with a man's arms coming back over the side of a boat, wet and dirty.
We don't know what he's retrieved from the river until Dickens tells us — almost as an afterthought.
And then comes a sentence of extraordinary ritual compression.
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
That triple repetition — chinked, blew, spat — is incantatory, like a folk ritual over money pulled from a corpse.
In one gesture, Dickens has told us everything about this novel's central subject: money, death, and the obscene intimacy between them.
Eleanor is right to press on that gesture, and I'd add something from the historical record.
River-finders — mudlarks and body-retrievers — were a recognised if despised profession in Victorian London.
The law was ambiguous about what they could take from the drowned, which produced its own peculiar moral fog.
What strikes me is how Dickens captures that ambiguity in the physical details — the washing of arms, the washing of money.
It is not guilt exactly — more like professional habit.
The spitting for luck is the detail that clinches it: a man who has entirely normalised robbing the dead.
I would not dissent from any of that, but I think we risk missing what is most extraordinary about the passage if we read it only as social document.
Dickens is, first and foremost, establishing moral atmosphere — not depicting a trade.
The man washes his arms over the side, but money is washed in the same river from which it was taken.
There is something almost sacramental and entirely damning in that repetition — cleansing that cannot cleanse.
Dickens gives us, in miniature, the whole moral logic of the novel: that money obtained through death corrupts the rituals meant to redeem us.
Edmund, I think that's exactly right — and it prepares us for everything that follows structurally.
Because the novel builds itself in these recurring rhythms — death, retrieval, transformation, moral consequence.
When Gaffer himself becomes one of the retrieved, the architecture snaps shut with tremendous force.
Riderhood's cry is barely four words, but they carry the whole weight of that opening scene.
"'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'"
That's Dickensian closure at its most ruthless — the instrument of the river becomes its victim.
The novel has remembered its own opening and answered it.
That irony has real teeth when you consider Riderhood's relationship with Gaffer.
Riderhood had accused Gaffer, had pursued him — and the river delivered the body before Riderhood could do further harm.
The river, in the novel's moral economy, is a more efficient instrument of justice than any institution Dickens depicts.
Which, given his view of Victorian institutions, is perhaps the darkest joke in the book.
One doesn't need to invoke the state's failures to feel the moral weight here — though James's point is well taken.
What interests me more is that Dickens balances this gothic severity against passages of quite remarkable moral affirmation.
The Boffins are the great counterweight in the architecture Eleanor describes.
Dickens's narrator makes a statement that is almost Burkean in its confidence about the nature of goodness.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That is not a sociological observation — it is a statement of moral theology.
And it is delivered with the narrative assurance of a man who has considered it and believes it.
That sentence is structurally fascinating to me, because it has the shape of an aphorism but the weight of an argument.
Dickens earns it — he's just given us ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities, and vanities in the woman.
The Boffins are deliberately not idealised — they are ignorant and unpolished, as the narrator says without apology.
That is what makes the moral claim land so hard.
Dickens doesn't argue that goodness belongs to the refined — he argues it is structurally indestructible wherever it takes root.
And the context makes that claim pointed, not merely pious.
The hard wrathful and sordid nature that Dickens refers to had wrung as much work out of them as could be got — for as little money as could be paid.
That is a description of labour exploitation rendered with surgical precision.
Even that grinding system, Dickens says, was forced to recognise their moral straightness and respect it.
Which is either a consolation or an indictment — I'm not entirely sure Dickens himself decides.
That productive ambiguity — whether the novel consoles or indicts — feels like exactly the right note on which to pause.

What we've traced today is an architecture built on recurrence and contrast — the ritual theft of Gaffer's opening answered by Gaffer's own retrieval, the gothic river balanced against the Boffins' indestructible decency.
In our next segment, we'll follow the money further — into the dust heaps, the Veneerings' dining table, and the way Dickens makes wealth itself into a kind of corruption.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: Closing: Love, Gold, and Redemption in the Wreckage

utterances.text: We've spent this episode navigating the Thames mud, the legal chambers, the dusty Mounds — and now we arrive at the wreckage.
Our Mutual Friend is, at its heart, a novel about what money does to people — and what love might be able to undo.
We have three final passages to draw together — confession, identity, and extortion — and three perspectives on what they mean for the novel as a whole.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — and with Charley Hexam's extraordinary confrontation with Bradley Headstone.
What strikes me first about this passage is its rhetorical architecture — the way Charley builds his accusation in layers, each clause a step closer to the wound he can't quite name.
He says 'I don't say what,' 'I don't say how much,' 'I go no closer' — Dickens gives him these little disclaimers that simultaneously accuse and retreat.
It's the syntax of a boy who has learned that power sometimes comes from what you don't say.
And then he lands his actual charge — and it's devastating.
"You know that I took you with me to his chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of him, and made myself responsible for my opinion of you."
Charley has staked his own social ascent on Headstone's respectability — and now that gamble has collapsed.
The moral question at the heart of this scene is whether Charley's anger is righteous or simply self-interested — and Dickens, magnificently, refuses to decide for us.
Eleanor is quite right that Dickens refuses to settle the question — and I think that refusal is one of his deepest strengths.
Charley Hexam is a study in the corruption of the will by ambition — a boy who has substituted getting-on for goodness, and finds the two have come apart.
His complaint against Headstone — 'Is that your gratitude to me?' — is framed as moral outrage, but it is really a ledger entry.
Which brings me, if I may, to the Wegg and Venus passage — because there we see the same moral vocabulary of partnership and entitlement, stripped of all pretence.
Dickens gives Wegg the language of fraternity — 'comrade, brother, and partner' — while the scheme he proposes is nakedly parasitic.
"He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
There is a comic absurdity to Wegg's precision — his willingness to revise upward to two-thirds, three-fourths — that shades into something rather chilling.
Greed, in this novel, always speaks the language of reasonableness.
Edmund's phrase — 'greed speaks the language of reasonableness' — is, I think, the key to how the whole legal and commercial machinery of this novel actually works.
Wegg's scheme — let Boffin bear the expense of excavating the Mounds, then extort him at the moment of completion — is a precise parody of how Victorian speculative enterprise operated.
You put in the labour of others, you claim the profit as your own, and you dress the whole thing up in contractual language.
And notice the phrase Dickens gives him — 'abject moral bondage and slavery' — which is not metaphor but method.
"He should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions."
'Purchase his freedom' — Dickens is deliberately invoking the vocabulary of enslavement, and applying it to the operations of capital.
That is not a casual word choice — not in 1865, not anywhere.
And that moral corruption runs all the way down, doesn't it — even to the confessional moment Riderhood fabricates on the river.
What is extraordinary about the Riderhood passage is that Dickens gives him this elaborate, almost fussy scrupulousness about exact words.
He hedges — 'I think he said in a score, but of that I am not positive, so take the lowest figure' — as if the arithmetic of false testimony matters.
And then he delivers what purports to be Gaffer's confession — and the simplicity of it is almost unbearable.
"There was foul play then. I done it for his money. Don't betray me!"
Three sentences, three facts — act, motive, plea — and Dickens strips the confession down to its bones precisely because it is invented.
Riderhood is a craftsman of lies, and Dickens respects the craft enough to render it perfectly.
The word 'betray' is doing considerable work in this novel — Riderhood uses it, Charley uses it implicitly, Wegg fears it.
And against all that — all that machinery of betrayal and avarice — Dickens places John Harmon's private reckoning with himself.
There is a passage I find genuinely moving — and I confess it surprises me that I do — in which Harmon rehearses his own motives with extraordinary self-suspicion.
"I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife."
That repetition of 'shrinking' — it is not weakness Dickens is depicting, but a kind of moral flinching that is the beginning of conscience.
Harmon is mistrustful even of himself — 'mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious' — and that is precisely what distinguishes him from every villain in this book.
The greedy ones never ask whether they are growing greedy.
That passage also documents something historically precise — the inheritance system that could compel a man to marry a stranger as the price of his father's fortune.
Harmon's father has, from beyond the grave, arranged a transaction — a daughter exchanged for a legacy.
And Harmon names the thing exactly: 'mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife' — the suspicion runs in both directions.
He cannot know whether Bella is mercenary, because the arrangement makes every response she gives him unreadable.
This is what inherited wealth actually does — it poisons the well of ordinary human trust.
And what redeems Harmon — what redeems the whole novel, I'd argue — is that Dickens insists on the reality of love even inside that poisoned system.
Harmon's self-examination ends with that wonderful Dickensian device — the character speaking to himself in the second person.
'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon.'
The man literally commands himself to be honest — to interrogate his own motives the way Riderhood never would, the way Wegg never could.
That moral seriousness — that willingness to be one's own severest witness — is what distinguishes the novel's redeemed characters from its damned ones.
The greedy ones never ask whether they are growing greedy — and the ones who do ask, who really face the question, are the ones who survive with their souls intact.
That feels like the moral spine of the whole novel, and I think you've three found it together.
Our Mutual Friend is not, finally, a novel about money — it is a novel about the courage required to refuse money's definitions of you.
My thanks to Dr Eleanor Hartley, Professor James Blackstone, and Sir Edmund Leigh — for a conversation as rich as the Mounds themselves, and rather more illuminating.
Until next time — keep reading, keep questioning, and watch where you step on the riverbank.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly
      witnessed, very short. Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever
      had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the

c65:p104.text:
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with
      the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more
      haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being
      overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair
      degenerating.
c65:p104.summary: Bradley sits all night in rigid despair, his face aging, whitening, and degenerating as if being consumed by internal fire while Riderhood maintains his vigilance.

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.
c19:p76.best_quote: 'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.
c31:p109.best_quote: Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And

c29:p3.text:
As some dogs have it in the blood, or are trained, to worry certain
      creatures to a certain point, so—not to make the comparison
      disrespectfully—Pleasant Riderhood had it in the blood, or had been
      trained, to regard seamen, within certain limits, as her prey. Show her a
      man in a blue jacket, and, figuratively speaking, she pinned him
      instantly. Yet, all things considered, she was not of an evil mind or an
      unkindly disposition. For, observe how many things were to be considered
      according to her own unfortunate experience. Show Pleasant Riderhood a
      Wedding in the street, and she only saw two people taking out a regular
      licence to quarrel and fight. Show her a Christening, and she saw a little
      heathen personage having a quite superfluous name bestowed upon it,
      inasmuch as it would be commonly addressed by some abusive epithet: which
      little personage was not in the least wanted by anybody, and would be
      shoved and banged out of everybody’s way, until it should grow big enough
      to shove and bang. Show her a Funeral, and she saw an unremunerative
      ceremony in the nature of a black masquerade, conferring a temporary
      gentility on the performers, at an immense expense, and representing the
      only formal party ever given by the deceased. Show her a live father, and
      she saw but a duplicate of her own father, who from her infancy had been
      taken with fits and starts of discharging his duty to her, which duty was
      always incorporated in the form of a fist or a leathern strap, and being
      discharged hurt her. All things considered, therefore, Pleasant Riderhood
      was not so very, very bad. There was even a touch of romance in her—of
      such romance as could creep into Limehouse Hole—and maybe sometimes
      of a summer evening, when she stood with folded arms at her shop-door,
      looking from the reeking street to the sky where the sun was setting, she
      may have had some vaporous visions of far-off islands in the southern seas
      or elsewhere (not being geographically particular), where it would be good
      to roam with a congenial partner among groves of bread-fruit, waiting for
      ships to be wafted from the hollow ports of civilization. For, sailors to
      be got the better of, were essential to Miss Pleasant’s Eden.
c29:p3.summary: Despite her predatory nature toward sailors and cynical views of life's ceremonies and relationships shaped by abuse, Pleasant Riderhood retains romantic dreams of escaping to distant islands.

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’

      him half a dozen times, ‘and I played it long ago; long afore you tried
      your clumsy hand at it; in days when you hadn’t begun croaking your
      lecters or what not in your school. I know to a figure how you done it.

      than you. I know how you come away from London in your own clothes, and
      where you changed your clothes, and hid your clothes. I see you with my
      own eyes take your own clothes from their hiding-place among them felled
      trees, and take a dip in the river to account for your dressing yourself,
      to any one as might come by. I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master,
      where you sat down Bargeman. I see you pitch your Bargeman’s bundle into
      the river. I hooked your Bargeman’s bundle out of the river. I’ve got your
      Bargeman’s clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained
      green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the
      blows. I’ve got them, and I’ve got you. I don’t care a curse for the
      T’other governor, alive or dead, but I care a many curses for my own self.
      And as you laid your plots agin me and was a sly devil agin me, I’ll be

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.

These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
